messages.subject: Re: 1 object detected from 2 points
messages.body_plain:
Just to add briefly to Tiago's comments:

Sometimes, point transect surveys are conducted on small study sites, in
which case points may be sufficiently close together for the same bird to
be recorded from more than one point, even if it doesn't move.  This is a
mild violation of the assumption of independent detections, but the
methods are robust to much stronger violations, so this is of no concern.
It does not introduce bias.  Consider these 3 cases:

1. A single bird is recorded twice from the same point on the same visit.
Counting a single visit as an effort of 1, this bird contributes twice to
the 'encounter rate' - birds detected per point per visit.  But the effort
is only recorded once - a single visit.  Hence double counting causes
bias.

2. A single bird is recorded once on each of 2 visits to the same
point.  Hence the effort is 2, and although the bird is counted twice, its
contribution to birds detected per point per visit is just one, not two as
occurs in case 1.  This doesn't generate bias.

3. A single visit is made to each point, and a bird is recorded once from
each of 2 points.  Effort again is 2 (1 visit to each of 2 points), and
the bird is counted twice.  Again, its contribution to birds detected per
point per visit is one, and this doesn't cause bias.

Steve

Hi All,

A while ago Russ Norvell asked about running the Distance analysis engine from
within other programming environments (below).  I replied to him, but he didn't
summarize the replies he got to the list yet, so I thought I'd put my message on
the list as it may help others (see below).  (Russ - could you please post any
other useful information you've gleaned?)

I've also written a very short Visual Basic project which gives an example of
one approach (that of making calls to the windows API).  You can find it on the
Distance web site, under Distance Support | General.  Hope someone finds it
useful!

 - Len

> >Distance analysis engine in order to run 1000's of simulations,
> >bootstraps, etc.  I've been through the List archive and seen a couple
> >suggestive posts, but nothing to imply that these have been brought to
> >fruition.

> >We'd like to look at the (admittedly retrospective) effects of
> >different study designs on estimates of annual bird density.  To start,
> >we hope to look at the effect of number of survey visits within a
> >breeding season (up to 5 at a given study site) and number of point
> >transect sub-samples (up to 10 at a given study site) on our annual
> >density estimates.  I suspect someone has already accomplished much of
> >this, but if not I'll ask around for a proper programmer.

> >Any thoughts?  Thanks in advance

Hi Russell,

I'm replying just to you (not the list) to give you a few leads and provide you
with the info I can -- please can you collate all the information you get and
forward it to the list at some point, so others can benefit -- thanks!

Okay, first to others who I know of - only two I'm afraid:

- Paul Luckacs at Colorado State developed some simulation software, WebSim, to
look at the optimal spacing of traps in trapping web studies.  In that he
simulates data and then calls the Distance analysis engine (D4.exe) to do the
analysis.  The program is written in C++ I think.  You can find out more, and
contact Paul, via his web page http://www.cnr.colostate.edu/~plukacs/web.html

- Tiago Marques here at St Andrews developed some quick and dirty code to do a
double platform analysis for someone in the Sea Mammal Research Unit here.  The
code does a special type of bootstrap and for each bootstrap rep calls D4.exe to
do the analysis.  It's written in VB.  Tiago is a student here, and you can get
his email address from the Directory page of the school web site
http://www-maths.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/

Secondly, as to how you might go about it (assuming you want to/have to develop
code from scratch).

As you probably know, the CDS and MCDS analysis engine live in a separate
executable file D4.exe (written in FORTRAN), which is in the Distance program
directory.  When you call D4.exe you pass in the location of a text file called
the command file which contains a bunch of lines of text telling distance what
analysis to do and also where a second file called the data file lives.  The
data file (obviously enough) contains the data to use in that analysis, in "flat
file" format.  All that happens when you press the "Run" button in Distance is
that Distance generates the appropriate files and then calls D4.exe.  This is
documented in the online help on the page "Running the analysis engines as a
stand-alone program" (towards the end of Chapter 8).

Probably the best way to see what the command and data files should look like is
to get Distance to generate a template.  In Distance, if you choose Tools |
Preferences and then the Analysis tab, and then tick the box "Debug mode", the
next time you run an analysis, Distance will generate the command and data
files, but will not run the analysis engine.  In the Log tab of the Analysis
details, Distance will tell you where it's put the files (usually in your temp
directory) so you can have a look at them.  The format of the command file is
pretty-much documented in the Distance 2.2 Users Guide, which you can download
from the Distance web site (under Distance 2.2).  There have been a few changes:
- in batch mode (what we're using) the output files are not given in ASSIGN
statements but in the first few lines of the command file (as documented in the
online help page)
- the flat file format for the data file
- there are some new commands for MCDS analyses
The best way to get a handle on these last two is to generate some template
files as described above and see what's in them.  One of these days I'll get
'round to writing an updated command manual... Meanwhile if you get problems
just drop me a line.

In many simulation applications, what you want to do is generate lots of
datasets, run the same analysis on each one, store the results, and then do some
summary statistics on the results.  If you really want to run the same analysis
on each simulated dataset, then you just need to get Distance to generate the
right template command file and just use that -- otherwise your program will
have to write its own command file which can be trickier.  In any case you will
have to write the data to a text file in the flat file format D4.exe expects --
you can put it where you like so long as you edit the INFILE command in the
command file.  As for harvesting results, D4.exe puts out results into two
files: the results file and the stats file.  The former is the long text file
that Distance displays in the Results page of the Analysis Details.  The second
is a compact fixed-format summary (Distance harvests these results and uses them
to put out the summary statistics in the Analysis Browser -- but you don't need
to know that!).  I suggest you use the latter as it is much easier to write a
program to parse this file.  The format of the stats file is documented in the
online help on the page "Saving Results to File" (Chapter 8).  You can also try
running an analysis from the command line, using the template files you've got
Distance to output, and then check out what it looks like for yourself.

Last thing is how to get your simulation program to run D4.exe.  Most computer
languages have a "shell" command or some such, which allows them to run
programs.  One problem with these is that often they start the external program
and then return control immediately to the calling routine.  In your situation
you'd rather have something that waited for the analysis to finish before
returning.  One solution (implemented by Tiago) is to simply have a "pause"
command and the next command after shell, causing the program to wait for a few
seconds before continuing -- in the hope that D4.exe will have finished by then.
This is simple, but a bit kludgy.  A second alternative is to use Windows API
(application programming interface - a lowish-level interface to Windows) to do
it -- this takes some knowledge of how to program the Windows API.  (Hint, if
you do go down this route: if you run D4.exe with CreateProcess (and then
WaitForInputIdle), you can wait for it to finish using WaitForSingleObject with
the timeout set to INFINITY.)  A third way is to use the .dll which I've already
written to do the job (it's called D4CDSNEI.dll - NEI is short for numerical
engine interface).  It is event driven, so you call a RunEngine method and then
wait for an event called RunFinished to fire.  If you're writing in an event
driven language such as VB then that's probably the easiest way.  I've put some
more information about this option at the bottom of this message, and can send
the source code if this would help.

Hope this helps to get you started -- if you have any more questions then give
me a shout.  If you get desperate, I can probably do the programming (or at
least the bulk of it which you can then modify) as a short contract.

 - Len

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Using D4CDSNEI.dll

It is an ActiveX dll, so any language that talks ActiveX will be able to use it.
For example, in a Visual Basic project, you choose Project | References, and
scroll down until you see "Distance 4 CDS Numerical Engine Interface" and tick
the box by that entry.  Then, if you use the VB object browser, you will see
that D4CDSNEI contains a class called CDSProcess, with methods RunEngine and
KillEngine, a property ErrMsg and an event RunFinished.  I've put the
documentation from my code below you can see more about the class.  I can send
all the code if you think it would be useful -- the rest of that .dll contains
stuff for getting settings out of a model definition and data filter and combing
them to make a command file, for putting together a data file, for calling
CDSProcess, and for parsing the results, stats and plot file to store results.

'-------------------------------------------------------------------------
'CDS Numerical Engine Process class - CDSProcess
'-------------------------------------------------------------------------

'Purpose: Class that represent the analysis engine process.  Contains
' API routines that start the analysis and wait for it to finish.  Also
' routines to stop it if necessary.

'This class is declared as public because it is not only used internally
' by CDSNEngineInterface, but it is also used in the Distance interface/
' project database for importing old D22 data.

'Interface:
' Properties:
'  ErrMsg As String (read-only)
'    If Status Is FileError Then
'    should contain an error message giving information about
'    where the error occured - this could be saved into the Log file.
' Methods:
'  RunEngine (EngineFile As String,
'    Infile As String, Optional ByVal Import As Boolean = False,
'    Optional ByVal CommandLineFile As String="")
'    - Starts the engine run - set Import to true if you want to import
'      an old distance file
'    - EngineFile is the exe name -- without the path (assume the engine
'      is located in App.Path)
'    - CommandLineFile is a file to put command line output into if
'      the engine is run under WinNT
'  KillEngine - Stops a run and kills the engine process
' Events:
'  RunFinished (EngineStatus As CDSEngineStatus)
'    - Raised when a run has finished.

Hi Scott,

I'm cc'ing my reply to the distance-sampling list as this is a question that
comes up fairly often:

On Wed, 10 Dec 2003 09:33:50 -0600, Scott Somershoe wrote:

> >Len,
> >   Thanks again for your help.  I think things are rolling smoothly now.
> >One question, I get a warning saying "Parameters are being constrained to
> >obtain monotonicity."  Is this a problem I need to worry about?

The short answer is usually not.

Here's the long answer.  Under most circumstances we expect a priori that true
detection function is a monotonicly non-increasing function of distance from the
point or line (i.e., the further the object is from the point or line, the lower
the probabilty of detection).  Therefore, by default, Distance tries to ensure
that the fitted function is monotonic non-increasing.  It does this by
evaluating the detection function g(x) at a set of evenly spaced distances (x's)
from 0 (x0) to the truncation distance (x9), and it makes sure that g(x0)>=g
(x1)>=g(x2)>=... >= g(x9).  There are other options in Model Definition |
Detection function | Constraints, and these are documented in the online manual.

Under most circumstances, the fitted function does not come up against this
constraint -- in other words the data indicate that the function should be
monotonic non-increasing.  However, under some circumstances the data call for a
non-monotonic function, so the constraint is triggered and that is why you get
the warning message.  The estimates you end up with are no longer maximum
likelihood estimates, but are constrained maximum likelihood estimates.

The commonest case where this happens is where you have a relatively small
dataset and just by chance there is a small "bump" at some distance, which
Distance would try to fit with an extra adjustment term, were it not for the
monotonicity constraint.  Such models are usually over-parameterized (too many
adjustment terms) and are not chosen using model selection criteria such as AIC.
You can see this in the D4Ducknest example project -- the half-normal+cosine
model gives a monotonicity warning when the first cosine term is added, but then
that model has an AIC of 1.5 worse than the plain half-normal model, so is not
selected.   See the Model Fitting page of results for that analysis. (If you
want to see the effect of the constraint, try running an analysis with half-
normal + 1 cosine adjustment manually selected and no constraints.)

You can also get this occuring where there is a problem in your dataset such as
evasive movement of animals, which leads to "too few" animals close to the line
or point, and "too many" away from it.  In this case, you don't want to fit the
data, but instead you want your fitted detection function to be "too high" close
to the line or point and "too low" away from it.  Fitting a hazard rate or half-
normal key function with few or no adjustments and monotonicity constraint
turned on will achieve this.  (An alternative with such data is to put the data
into intervals, as I think has been discussed in previous postings.)

If a function that has been constrained is the one selected by Distance then
there is a minor problem with the estimate of the variance of f(0).  This is
because the fit is no longer the maximum likelihood fit (because of the
constraint) so the theory used in deriving the variance isn't valid.  However,
in practice this isn't something to worry about.  In any case, we recommend
deriving final variance estimates for D or N using a nonparametric bootstrap,
resampling by transects, so the analytic variance of f(0) becomes irrelevant.

So, in summary, if you see this message, you should look at the Model Fitting
page of results to see which function it was fitting when the message occured.
Was that function selected?  If not, it's likely just a symptom that the model
not selected had too many parameters.  Also look again at your data and ask
yourself why was the constraint hit -- is there some problem in your data (such
as evasive movement), or was it likely due to one histogram bar being slightly
higher than previous bars just due to chance (as with the Ducknest data).  The
histogram plots and Chi-sq goodness of fit tests will be useful in answering
this.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

Hi Smita, (cc distance-sampling list)

Thanks for sending your project file to me.  I had a look and there several
important issues to discuss.  However, first to your questions:

> >I am using DISTANCE to analyse some transect data for large mammals and
> >got the following warnings
> >1: convergence failure
> >2: analysis engine wrote some output to the console error stream
> >fortl: error63 output conversion error unit 3
> >Ihave no idea how to tackle these. could someone help me.

Convergence failure
===================

If you look through the Detection Function/Global/Model Fitting pages, you will
find the entry that says:

-----------------------------------------------------
 Model  6
    Negative Exponential key, k(y) = Exp(-y/A(1))
    Cosine adjustments of order(s) :  1, 2, 3, 4, 5
       Results:
       Convergence was NOT achieved with  609 function evaluations.
 Maximum number of iterations exceeded.
       Final Ln(likelihood) value =  -7408.6353
       Akaike information criterion =   14829.271
       Bayesian information criterion =   14861.627
       AICc =   14829.322
       Final parameter values:   13.614106      15.358477     -37.528488
35.342670
                                 -18.444685      4.4927039
      ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **
      ** Warning: Some parameters are very highly correlated. **

    Likelihood ratio test between models  5 and  6
       Likelihood ratio test value    =  -111.1388
       Probability of a greater value =   1.000000
 *** Model  5 selected over model  6 based on minimum AIC
-----------------------------------------------------

This means that the maximum likelihood algorithm could not find the maximum for
that model -- it gave up after 609 steps.  If we were interested in looking in
more detail we could ask Distance to output more details of the fitting (under
Model Definition | Misc, tick Report results for each iteration of detection
function fitting routine), and we could think about trying different starting
values (under Model Definition | Detection Function | Adustment terms).
However, in this case I don't think it's worth it because:
- I would not fit the negative exponential function to your data (see below)
- we also need to think about other issues such as trunction first (see below)
- problems like this tend to occur when there are a large number of adjustment
terms; 5 adjustment terms is almost certainly too many for the data set - after
truncation and using a different key function I'm sure less will be selected.  I
don't think I've ever used a model with 5 adjustment terms in an analysis!

As an aside, you notice that it selected model 5 (the one with 4 adjustment
terms) over this model based on AIC -- although if it had found the maximum of
the likelihood  it may have chosen model 6.

Output conversion error
=======================

When you get this error, it is because Distance tries to write a number to the
results file that is too long to fit in its allocated slot.  For example, if I
only allowed 5 spaces for an AIC value, and the value was 100001 (ie 6
characters long), then it would not fit in the space allowed.  Then, all you
will get in the space is "****", and you'll also see an output conversion error.

Looking through the model fitting results, I see the following entry:
-----------------------------------------------------
 Model  5
    Uniform key, k(y) = 1/W
    Cosine adjustments of order(s) :  1, 2, 3, 4
       Results:
       Convergence was achieved with    9 function evaluations.
       Final Ln(likelihood) value =  -32352.110
       Akaike information criterion =   64712.223
       Bayesian information criterion =   64733.793
       AICc =   64712.246
       Final parameter values:  -10.910233     -9.5199814     -2.3730536     -
4.2617893

      ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **

    Likelihood ratio test between models  4 and  5
       Likelihood ratio test value    = **********
       Probability of a greater value =   1.000000
 *** Model  4 selected over model  5 based on minimum AIC
-----------------------------------------------------

Can you spot the ****s?  The log likelihood for model 4 in this case is
-7445.7620 -- which is an enormous distance from the log-likelihood for model 5
(I expect the difference is because of the constraints being triggered in model
5).  The likelihood ratio is -2(lnL1-lnL2), which in this case is 49812.696 -- I
guess this larger than I'd been banking on, so causing the error.

Other important issues
======================

- I notice you haven't truncated your data.  As you will read in both the online
manual and the distance sampling book, it's almost always a good idea do some
data trunction.  This reduces the number of adjustment terms required, and tends
to lead to more reliable results.

- I would not use the negative exponential key function, unless you have a
specific reason to do so.  It does not have a "shoulder" so violates the shape
criterion.  See the distance sampling book for details.

- I would not try to fit 4 key functions in one analysis.  Rather (after
truncation), I would try 3 different analyses with 3 different key functions,
and then compare the results.  The advantage of doing this is that you get the
detection function histograms and goodness-of-fit tests for each of the models,
and can look at other criteria as well as the AIC.

- I notice you have only one transect line in this analysis.  I hope you had
more in reality in the field, otherwise the study design is deeply flawed.  If
you had more, you should enter them in the project, otherwise the variance due
to encounter rate will be calculated incorrectly, and so the overall variance of
your density estimate will be wrong.

Invitation to others on the list
================================

Unfortunately, I don't have time to go into each of the above issues in detail
with you.  Perhaps there is someone else on the list who would be willing to
answer any questions you may have about these -- they are also the kind of thing
covered in the Introduction to Distance book and on our workshops.  I'll leave
any kind souls to contact you directly!  Perhaps if you do get some good help,
you or whoever helps could post a summary of the analysis and your conclusions
to the list so we can all learn from it!

Cheers,

 - Len
